canonical_title: Removing a named-provider single point of failure from a mandatory verification gate is a distinct move from weakening the gate itself -- both must be proven separately
summary: Source 18 previously hard-coded Claude Code as Stage 19 owner and explicitly marked Codex 'Not verifier'. SB-GOV-IV-1.0 replaced that hard-coded ownership with a 'Mission Control-appointed Independent Verification Actor' role, removing the single-provider dependency, while simultaneously and explicitly preserving Stage 19 as mandatory, preserving actor separation, preserving human runtime verification, and preserving Mission Control acceptance authority. The distinction 'Codex Not Required != Independent Verification Not Required' was written into the approved design, the amendment, and the activation record to prevent the two changes from being conflated.

claims.text: The Founder-approved architecture explicitly lists what actor-flexibility must preserve alongside the new appointed-actor role: no self-verification, actual contribution separation, capability fit, explicit Mission Control appointment, preserved human runtime verification, preserved Mission Control runtime review, preserved Stage 19, preserved Evidence Package/Completion Report ownership, preserved Mission Control acceptance, and preserved Founder authority.

evidence.locator: 'Approved architecture': 'The lifecycle role becomes: Mission Control-appointed Independent Verification Actor subject to: no self-verification; actual contribution separation; capability fit; explicit Mission Control appointment; preserved human runtime verification; preserved Mission Control runtime review; preserved Stage 19; ... preserved Mission Control acceptance; preserved Founder authority.'

claims.text: The distinction between Codex's own utilization classification and the mandatory Stage 19 lifecycle gate was stated as a 'critical interpretation' at activation, not merely as a drafting note: 'Codex Not Required != Independent Verification Not Required', with Stage 19 confirmed as remaining mandatory and owned by the Mission Control-appointed Independent Verification Actor, subject to actual contribution separation, capability fit, explicit appointment, no self-verification, no self-approval and preserved higher-authority gates.

evidence.locator: Section 2, 'Source 18 v1.1': 'Stage 19 remains mandatory and is owned by: Mission Control-appointed Independent Verification Actor subject to actual contribution separation, capability fit, explicit appointment, no self-verification, no self-approval and preserved higher-authority gates.' Section 3, 'Critical interpretation: Codex Not Required != Independent Verification Not Required'.

claims.text: Codex remains the preferred independent verifier for the highest-risk cases under the active protocol, but the protocol's own text states this preference explicitly alongside the statement that no provider becomes an architectural single point of failure -- preference and structural dependency were kept as two different things, not treated as the same claim.

evidence.locator: Section 2: 'Current Source 18 assigns Stage 19 to Claude Code and its Appendix A says Codex is Not verifier. All SB-P-* missions retain that assignment and mandatory gate until a Founder-approved amendment is activated. A Codex budget is neither Stage 19 authorization nor permission to omit Stage 19.'

conditions: Applies when replacing a hard-coded single-provider dependency in a mandatory gate with an appointable/flexible role, where the goal is resilience against provider unavailability, not a reduction in verification rigor.

Requires the preserved-invariant list (mandatory gate, actor separation, human runtime review, acceptance authority) to be stated explicitly at every stage of the change -- design recommendation, Founder approval, and activation -- so flexibility cannot later be misread as having also relaxed the gate.
anti_patterns: Treating 'this provider is not strictly required' as equivalent to 'this verification step is not required' -- the two are easy to conflate once a named-provider requirement becomes a flexible role, and this mission's records deliberately wrote the distinction down at each stage to prevent that conflation.

Removing a named-provider dependency without an explicit, Founder-level decision when the provider was originally named by governance -- an ad hoc or silent substitution would have bypassed the actor-separation and capability-fit review this mission's design explicitly required.
